O.outcome_detail: reported cramming less

cells.quote: As the study notes, after the LHTL intervention, “… students of the experimental group reported cramming less, using more learning techniques, redoing exercises with answers covered, and spacing repetitions more often instead of massing.
cells.note: The study text reports the direction but does not describe the comparison condition, assignment method, or effect size.

O.outcome_detail: final proficiency test of the second semester

cells.quote: Students ’online study behavior veri ﬁed their answers to the questionnaire and showed a more ef ﬁcient use of the learning platforms. Students also bene ﬁted from this intervention by scoring higher in the ﬁnal pro ﬁciency test of the second semester.”
cells.note: The study text reports higher final-test scores but does not describe the comparison condition, assignment method, or effect size.

O.outcome_detail: public review count as a rough proxy for comparative enrollment and popularity

cells.quote: It is often dif ﬁcult to ﬁnd comparative enrollment numbers, but the number of public reviews on a general MOOC review platform can serve as a rough proxy. On Class Central ( https://www.class-central.com), one of the most widely used MOOC review platforms, LHTL has 6712 reviews, while the few other more general learning-related courses have far fewer: Athabasca University ’s “Learning to Learn Online ”has 5 reviews, and Monash University ’s “Introduction to Psychology: The Psychology of Learning ” and Stanford ’s “Reading to Learn in Science”each have 1 (as of March 2019).
cells.note: The study treats public review counts as a rough proxy for comparative enrollment and uses them to argue that LHTL was substantially more popular than the named comparison MOOCs; this is not a randomized comparison.

D.treatment: existing LHW maternal-health training and role

O.outcome_detail: readiness to identify and manage pre-eclampsia and eclampsia

cells.quote: Findings from this study demonstrate that the existing LHW program could provide a platform for community-based identification and management of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia in Pakistan with the help of the existing network of LHWs.
cells.note: The study explored potential rather than testing an educational intervention; no direct treatment-comparison effect was reported.

D.treatment: identifying danger signs of seizures in pregnancy
D.comparison: identifying danger signs of hypertension in pregnancy

O.outcome_detail: affirmative self-reported competency

cells.quote: Identify danger signs of hypertension in pregnancy	331 (72 %)
cells.note: The questionnaire reported a higher affirmative response for identifying seizure danger signs than hypertension danger signs; this was not a randomized educational comparison.

O.outcome_detail: self-reported confidence

cells.quote: LHWs expressed confidence in basic skills in providing maternal care: 34 % were confident in measuring BP and 87 % were confident in administering intramuscular injections.
cells.note: This is a within-questionnaire contrast between reported competencies, not an instructional treatment comparison.

D.treatment: training and equipment for pre-eclampsia screening and emergency management

O.outcome_detail: capacity to screen, treat and refer women

cells.quote: However, the implementation needs to be combined with appropriate training, equipment availability and supervision.
cells.note: The study identified implementation requirements but did not measure an outcome after training, equipment provision or supervision.

O.outcome_detail: perceived need for training on pre-eclampsia and eclampsia

cells.quote: Many LHSs recognised the need for training, with a focus on identifying woman at high-risk. Also, they claimed that pre-eclampsia and eclampsia are very important subjects; however, they had received negligible attention during their training. In contrast, very few TBAs perceived the need to learn about pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.
cells.note: The contrast is based on qualitative focus group discussions and concerns participants' perceived need for training, not an evaluated learning intervention.

O.outcome_detail: management approach for suspected or confirmed hypertension in pregnancy

cells.quote: LHWs do not carry any antihypertensive agents for pregnant women; in cases of suspected or confirmed hypertension they refer to the nearest public facility.
cells.note: The study describes current practice and proposes task-sharing; it does not evaluate a comparative intervention outcome.

O.outcome_detail: ability to measure blood pressure

cells.quote: LHWs expressed confidence in basic skills in providing maternal care: 34 % were confident in measuring BP and 87 % were confident in administering intramuscular injections.
cells.note: The study reports a descriptive proportion, not a treatment-versus-comparison contrast.

D.treatment: self-reported confidence in administering intramuscular injections

O.outcome_detail: ability to administer intramuscular injections

cells.quote: LHWs expressed confidence in basic skills in providing maternal care: 34 % were confident in measuring BP and 87 % were confident in administering intramuscular injections.

O.outcome_detail: reported receipt of training

cells.quote: Around 44 % of LHWs mentioned receiving training to identify pregnancy complications while 56 % mentioned receiving training to refer or manage pregnancy complication (Table 2).
cells.note: The study reports training receipt descriptively and does not provide a treatment-versus-comparison contrast.

O.outcome_detail: Knowledge of diarrhoea and pneumonia classification and assessment

cells.quote: Similar findings emerged from FGDs and IDIs conducted with LHSs. However, LHSs were able to comment more comprehensively on the types of diarrhoea and method for assessing dehydration.
cells.note: The study compares participant groups in qualitative interviews rather than assigning a learning treatment.

D.treatment: Adequate supportive supervision and LHS presence during household visits

O.outcome_detail: Perceived LHW performance in iCCM

cells.quote: LHWs considered adequate supervision and the presence of LHSs during household visits as a factor facilitating their performance.
cells.note: This is a perceived facilitator reported in interviews, not a controlled comparison.

O.outcome_detail: Knowledge, performance and motivation for iCCM

cells.quote: According to health workers further training would improve LHWs’ knowledge, performance, motivation and LHSs’ supervision.
cells.note: The direction reflects participants’ stated expectations; the study did not measure a training effect experimentally.

O.outcome_detail: Perceived usefulness of feedback for improving LHW performance

cells.quote: LHWs did not have a preference for written or verbal feedback, but LHSs considered written individual feedback to LHWs to be more useful than group and verbal feedback.
cells.note: Preferences differed between LHWs and LHSs, so the reported direction is mixed rather than a measured performance advantage.

D.treatment: adequate supervision with LHS accompaniment during household visits
D.comparison: less frequent supervision or no accompanied field visits

O.outcome_detail: LHW performance in community case management

cells.quote: LHWs considered adequate supervision and the presence of LHSs during household visits as a factor facilitating their performance.
cells.note: The study reports participants’ perspectives rather than an experimental comparison.

O.outcome_detail: community recognition of the health-worker role

cells.quote: Many participants reported that the community recognizes LHWs as “vaccinators” because they visit households for polio campaigns. Therefore, LHWs have become more recognized for their polio work than their designated LHW-P responsibilities.
cells.note: This is a qualitative comparison of perceived community recognition, not a tested intervention effect.

O.outcome_detail: LHW credibility and motivation to perform

cells.quote: The motivation of all LHWs and LHSs is significantly hampered by the lack of supplies and medicines. A considerable number of health workers highlighted the unavailability of ORS, zinc and antibiotics as a demotivating factor in terms of improving knowledge and performance. Health workers believe that the availability of medicines can strengthen their credibility in the community.
cells.note: The study reports participants’ perceived motivational and credibility consequences of medicine availability; no causal effect was estimated.
